query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Grain boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation, as revealed by atom probe tomography, are the primary mechanisms governing toughness degradation in initially single-phase high-entropy alloys.
generation.intervention: Controlled introduction of grain boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation
generation.conditions: High and low temperature, various loading conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation
generation.mechanism: Nanoscale mechanisms governing grain boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation
generation.predicted_outcome: Emergence of brittle behavior in high-entropy alloys due to grain boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation
generation.baseline: Initial toughness of the high-entropy alloy
generation.boundary: Service and loading boundaries of the high-entropy alloy
generation.uncertainty: Exact relationships between grain boundary segregation, brittle grain-boundary precipitation, and toughness degradation

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of high-entropy alloys with and without grain boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation, using atom probe tomography and mechanical testing
measurements: Toughness, grain boundary segregation, brittle grain-boundary precipitation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy without grain boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation exhibits similar toughness to the alloy with grain boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation, then the hypothesis is falsified.

decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has progressed from exploring their unique properties and potential applications to understanding the underlying mechanisms governing their behavior. Studies have investigated the effects of grain size, grain boundary segregation, and deformation mechanisms on the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys. Recent research has focused on developing new alloys with improved strength, ductility, and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement.
decision.unsolved: The exact mechanisms governing toughness degradation in high-entropy alloys remain unclear, and further research is needed to understand the relationships between grain boundary segregation, brittle grain-boundary precipitation, and rapid grain coarsening.
decision.why: To investigate the nanoscale mechanisms governing grain boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation, and to understand the relationships between these phenomena and toughness degradation in high-entropy alloys.
